floating-equality.title: Comparing floating-point values with ==
floating-equality.short: Two double values that should be equal can compare as false.
floating-equality.summary: Because many decimal fractions cannot be represented exactly in binary floating point, tiny rounding errors can remain after calculations.
floating-equality.why: Values such as 0.1 and 0.2 do not have finite exact representations in double, so their stored values include rounding error.
floating-equality.tips: Choose a tolerance based on the scale and precision your application actually needs. See [[equality]] for general equality behavior. For money, decimal may be a better fit.

badNotes.2: This compares double values directly with ==

goodNotes.3: Compare whether the difference is within an acceptable tolerance

integer-overflow.title: Integer overflow
integer-overflow.short: A large integer calculation can wrap to a different value without throwing.
integer-overflow.summary: In ordinary unchecked integer arithmetic, a result outside the type's range can wrap around. Use [[overflow-exception|checked]] when you want overflow to be detected as an exception.
integer-overflow.why: int has a fixed number of bits, so values beyond its representable range can leave only the low-order bits of the result.
integer-overflow.tips: For calculations that can grow large, decide whether using long is sufficient or whether checked should raise an [[overflow-exception|OverflowException]].

badNotes.2: The value wraps when it exceeds the int range

reference-equality.title: Confusing reference identity with value equality
reference-equality.short: Two objects with the same contents may still compare as different objects.
reference-equality.summary: For a class, which is a [[value-reference-types|reference type]], the default equality behavior may compare whether two references point to the same instance rather than whether their contents match.
reference-equality.why: A normal class does not treat separately created instances as equal values unless equality is defined appropriately.
reference-equality.tips: For types that should compare by value, consider [[records|record]] or implementing [[equality|Equals / GetHashCode]].

badNotes.4: A normal class compares these as separate instances

goodNotes.1: Use record when value-based equality matches the type's meaning

deferred-enumeration.title: Enumerating a LINQ query repeatedly
deferred-enumeration.short: A costly operation runs multiple times even though the same IEnumerable is reused.
deferred-enumeration.summary: A LINQ sequence with [[linq-deferred|deferred execution]] can run its source pipeline again every time it is enumerated.
deferred-enumeration.why: Count() and foreach each enumerate query from the beginning, so GetItems or IsValid can run repeatedly.
deferred-enumeration.tips: Materialize with ToList when repeated enumeration is actually a problem. That does not mean every [[ienumerable|IEnumerable]] should always be materialized.

badNotes.3: foreach enumerates the same query again

empty-statement-loop.title: A stray semicolon creates an empty loop
empty-statement-loop.short: The loop repeats an empty statement and the following block runs only once.
empty-statement-loop.summary: A semicolon immediately after while is a complete empty statement, so it becomes the loop body and disconnects the block that visually follows it.
empty-statement-loop.why: The bounded condition still advances i, but the block has separate [[scope]] and executes after the loop has already finished.
empty-statement-loop.tips: Remove the semicolon and use braces for the intended body, then verify the number and values of the observed iterations.

badNotes.2: This semicolon is the entire loop body

goodNotes.2: Without the semicolon, the following block belongs to the loop

negative-remainder.title: Negative remainders break circular indexing
negative-remainder.short: A negative dividend can produce a negative remainder and therefore an invalid index.
negative-remainder.summary: C# % computes a remainder whose sign follows the dividend; it is not a mathematical modulo operation that always returns a nonnegative result.
negative-remainder.why: With offset -1 and length 3, offset % length is -1, which cannot index the array.
negative-remainder.tips: Require a positive wrap length so the calculation does not encounter [[divide-by-zero|division by zero]], then normalize with (value % length + length) % length.

goodNotes.4: Reject a nonpositive wrap length before using %
goodNotes.5: The second remainder keeps the normalized index within bounds

mutable-struct-copy.title: Updating only a copy of a struct
mutable-struct-copy.short: A local value-type copy changes while the element stored in a collection does not.
mutable-struct-copy.summary: Reading a struct from List<T> returns its value. Mutating that local value cannot reach back into the list unless the changed struct is assigned to the element again.
mutable-struct-copy.why: item receives a copy of items[0], so incrementing item.Value changes only the local variable. The corrected code explicitly replaces the stored element.
mutable-struct-copy.tips: This follows [[value-reference-types|value-type copying]], not a List<T> defect. Prefer immutable structs or make the read-modify-write replacement visible.

badNotes.2: Reading the value-type element makes a local copy

goodNotes.2: Read the element value into a local
goodNotes.4: Write the complete changed value back into the list

record-shallow-copy.title: Record with expressions share nested collections
record-shallow-copy.short: A record copy is new, but referenced mutable children remain shared by default.
record-shallow-copy.summary: A with expression performs the record's generated shallow copy and then applies listed member changes. Reference-typed components are copied as references rather than recursively cloned.
record-shallow-copy.why: An empty with expression gives copy a new Order object whose Items still points to the original List<string>, so mutation is visible through both records.
record-shallow-copy.tips: Understand the generated [[records|with-copy operation]] before choosing independence. Copy nested collections explicitly, as shown, or store immutable children.

badNotes.2: The generated record copy reuses the Items reference
badNotes.3: This mutates the list shared with original

goodNotes.2: Replace Items with a new list containing the same elements
goodNotes.3: Only the copied order's list is mutated

closure-loop-capture.title: Capturing a loop variable gives callbacks the same value
closure-loop-capture.short: Deferred callbacks observe one for-loop variable after the loop has advanced.
closure-loop-capture.summary: A closure captures a variable rather than freezing its value. A for loop has one i variable, so callbacks invoked later all read its final value after the loop ends.
closure-loop-capture.why: Each bad callback closes over the same i, which has become 3 by invocation time. A local declared inside the body creates separate per-iteration storage.
closure-loop-capture.tips: A [[closures|captured variable]] is observed when the callback runs. Copy the current value into a new local when each deferred action needs its own snapshot.

badNotes.2: All iterations use the same i variable
badNotes.3: The lambda captures i rather than its current value

goodNotes.4: Each iteration creates a distinct current variable
goodNotes.5: The callback captures that iteration's storage

dictionary-duplicate-keys.title: Forgetting a duplicate-key policy in ToDictionary
dictionary-duplicate-keys.short: Two projected rows choose the same key and dictionary creation fails.
dictionary-duplicate-keys.summary: ToDictionary requires every projected key to be unique under its comparer and throws ArgumentException when it encounters a duplicate.
dictionary-duplicate-keys.why: Both rows use key 1. The correction groups them and explicitly chooses Last as the winner before creating one entry per key.
dictionary-duplicate-keys.tips: Use [[linq-groupby|GroupBy]] as the final representation when multiple values per key are valid; otherwise document whether duplicates are rejected or which value wins.

collection-modified-enumeration.title: Mutating a collection during enumeration
collection-modified-enumeration.short: A structural List change invalidates the active enumerator.
collection-modified-enumeration.summary: List<T>.Enumerator tracks the collection version. Adding or removing elements after enumeration begins invalidates that state and a later MoveNext throws InvalidOperationException.
collection-modified-enumeration.why: The bad loop removes from the same List it is traversing. RemoveAll performs the removal as one collection operation without an external enumerator.
collection-modified-enumeration.tips: The [[ienumerable|enumerator state]] represents one traversal, not a live cursor resilient to structural mutation; collect changes separately or use a suitable bulk operation.

mutable-hash-keys.title: Mutating a hash key makes entries unreachable
mutable-hash-keys.short: Changing equality-relevant state moves a key logically without rehashing it.
mutable-hash-keys.summary: A Dictionary chooses a bucket from the key's hash at insertion. Mutating fields used by equality or hashing can make later lookup inspect a different bucket.
mutable-hash-keys.why: Changing Code from A to B changes the same object's hash without relocating its stored entry. An immutable record key keeps membership stable.
mutable-hash-keys.tips: The [[custom-equality-hashing|hash and equality contract]] must remain consistent for the entire time a key belongs to a Dictionary or HashSet.

linq-orderby-reset.title: Repeated OrderBy calls replace the primary sort key
linq-orderby-reset.short: A second ordering starts over instead of adding a tie-breaker.
linq-orderby-reset.summary: OrderBy begins a new ordered sequence. Calling it again makes the new key primary and discards the prior key's role in the requested ordering.
linq-orderby-reset.why: ThenBy extends the Group ordering with Rank only inside equal groups, preserving the intended two-key contract.
linq-orderby-reset.tips: Use [[list-sort|OrderBy to begin an order]] and ThenBy or ThenByDescending to extend it with additional keys.

regex-escaping.title: Confusing string escaping with regex escaping
regex-escaping.short: Account for C# literal parsing and regex metacharacters as separate layers.
regex-escaping.summary: C# first interprets a regular or verbatim string literal, then the regex engine parses the resulting characters. User text can contain regex operators even when it is valid C# text.
regex-escaping.why: The [[string-literals|source-language interpretation]] happens before regex parsing; Regex.Escape quotes a runtime fragment for literal pattern matching.
regex-escaping.tips: Escape only the literal fragment, not a complete pattern whose operators you intend to keep. Use a finite matching timeout.

culture-sensitive-numbers.title: Culture-dependent numeric parsing changes values
culture-sensitive-numbers.short: Bind persisted numeric text to one documented separator policy.
culture-sensitive-numbers.summary: A comma can be a grouping separator in one culture and a decimal separator in another. CurrentCulture therefore can turn the same text into a different value or reject it.
culture-sensitive-numbers.why: Successful [[parse-number|numeric parsing]] alone does not prove the intended meaning; the culture and NumberStyles are part of the data contract.
culture-sensitive-numbers.tips: Use the same explicit culture for persisted input and output, and reserve user culture for genuinely localized display and entry.

timespan-component-totals.title: Confusing TimeSpan components with totals
timespan-component-totals.short: Use TotalHours or TotalMinutes for the complete elapsed quantity.
timespan-component-totals.summary: Hours and Minutes are components within the day and hour portions of a TimeSpan, so they wrap. TotalHours and TotalMinutes include the entire duration as fractional totals.
timespan-component-totals.why: The [[timespan-arithmetic|27.5-hour duration]] has Hours equal to 3 after one full day, but TotalHours remains 27.5.
timespan-component-totals.tips: Choose a component for formatted decomposition and a Total property for calculations or thresholds.

nan-infinity.title: Treating NaN and Infinity as ordinary numbers
nan-infinity.short: Detect non-finite floating-point results before ordinary comparison logic.
nan-infinity.summary: NaN compares unequal to every value, including itself, and ordered comparisons with NaN are false. Infinity can also pass through calculations unless the domain rejects it.
nan-infinity.why: Floating-point division by zero can produce NaN or infinity, unlike the integer failure described by [[divide-by-zero|DivideByZeroException]].
nan-infinity.tips: Use IsNaN, IsInfinity, or IsFinite explicitly. Define whether non-finite values are rejected, propagated, or represented separately.

date-interval-boundaries.title: Losing boundary data in date-range queries
date-interval-boundaries.short: Use start-inclusive, end-exclusive intervals in one time basis.
date-interval-boundaries.summary: A guessed last instant such as 23:59:59.999 misses values with finer precision. A half-open interval includes every representable instant from the start up to, but not including, the next boundary.
date-interval-boundaries.why: Derive the next calendar date with [[dateonly-timeonly|DateOnly]] instead of guessing the day's final time-of-day.
date-interval-boundaries.tips: The sample defines a UTC calendar day and compares UTC-based DateTimeOffset values. For a local calendar day, resolve both boundaries through the chosen time zone first.
